name: Corpse Candle
description: The Corpse Candle (Welsh canwyll corff) is a Welsh death omen: a small, pale, blue or yellow flame seen drifting along country lanes, churchyards, and the route a forthcoming funeral will take, foretelling the death of someone in the household it visits.
full_description: The Corpse Candle (Welsh canwyll corff or cannwyll corph, plural canhwyllau corff) is one of the most distinctive figures of Welsh death folklore: a small atmospheric flame, typically described as pale blue, yellow, or white, that drifts at walking pace along an ancient corpse road or lych-way, settles upon the door or window of a doomed house, or marks the route a funeral cortège will shortly take. According to Welsh tradition, the size and brilliance of the flame indicates the age and status of the person about to die — a small dim flame for a child, a brighter one for an adult — and multiple lights may foretell multiple deaths in the same family. The light may be seen by anyone, but particular families and women known as cannwyllwyr are said to have a hereditary gift for seeing them. The phenomenon is documented from at least the 17th century, with the most influential printed account being by the Welsh nonconformist minister Edmund Jones in A Relation of Apparitions of Spirits in the County of Monmouth and the Principality of Wales (1767). Corpse candles form part of a wider Welsh and Celtic 'death-warning' complex that also includes phantom funerals (toili), the cyhyraeth, and the gwrach-y-rhibyn. They are likely related to the same atmospheric ghost-lights known elsewhere as will-o'-the-wisp, ignis fatuus, jack-o'-lantern (English), spunkie (Scots), and feu follet (French). Modern scientific accounts attribute many such sightings to the oxidation of marsh-gas (methane and phosphine) over wetlands, with cold-flame chemistry, bioluminescence, and microlightning between methane bubbles in water proposed as further mechanisms; however, the strongly Welsh death-omen interpretation belongs entirely to folk tradition rather than to natural science.

aliases.name: Will-o'-the-wisp
aliases.meaning: Generic English term for similar atmospheric ghost lights

aliases.name: Ignis fatuus
aliases.meaning: 'Foolish fire'; learned name for the marsh-light phenomenon

origin: Strongly localised to Wales, with secondary occurrences across the Welsh Marches, Cornwall, and parts of Ireland and Scotland; the broader 'death-omen ghost-light' complex extends to most of Northern Europe and to colonial diasporas in the Americas.

etymology.origin: Welsh: canwyll ('candle') + corff ('body, corpse'). The phrase is a direct calque of the Latin candela mortis used in some medieval Welsh ecclesiastical sources.
etymology.first_use: Welsh-language oral usage long predates documentation; first widely circulated in print through Edmund Jones (1767) in English-language form.

timeline.event: Welsh Nonconformist minister Edmund Jones reports being born into a community where corpse-candle tradition is already universal (Jones lived 1702–1793; the tradition predates him by centuries)
timeline.source: Jones, E. (1767), A Relation of Apparitions of Spirits...

timeline.event: Richard Baxter, in The Certainty of the Worlds of Spirits, prints Welsh accounts of corpse candles
Edmund Jones publishes A Relation of Apparitions of Spirits in the County of Monmouth and the Principality of Wales
timeline.significance: Becomes the foundational printed source for the canwyll corff tradition

timeline.event: Jones reissues an expanded edition with further corpse-candle narratives
timeline.significance: Cements the literary canon of Welsh apparition lore

timeline.event: American journalist Wirt Sikes publishes British Goblins: Welsh Folk-Lore, Fairy Mythology, Legends, and Traditions, devoting substantial space to canwyll corff
timeline.significance: Brings the tradition to a wide Anglophone Victorian readership

timeline.event: Marie Trevelyan publishes Folk-Lore and Folk-Stories of Wales, including extensive corpse-candle material
timeline.significance: Most ambitious single Welsh-language and Anglo-Welsh folklore compendium of its era

timeline.event: T. Gwynn Jones, Welsh Folklore and Folk-Custom, is reissued, summarising and contextualising the canwyll corff

related.name: Cyhyraeth

related.name: Phantom Funeral (toili)
related.description: Welsh phantom funeral procession that often accompanies or follows the corpse-candle's route

cultural_notes: The canwyll corff is treated within Welsh tradition as a real and serious sign, neither lightly invoked nor mocked; the appropriate response is prayer and preparation for the death of a known parishioner.
